title: The eight limbs (2.29)
hook: one sutra lists eight limbs of yoga, from how you treat others to absorption, and only one of them is a posture
tomorrow: Yama — non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint, non-grasping

segments.voice: Yesterday: aviplava. Viveka, telling the seer from the seen, held steady. Did you try this is a thought, not a fact? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

A yoga studio timetable is taped up by the front desk. Halfway down: Ashtanga, six p.m. Bring water. Expect to sweat. That class is a real modern tradition of its own. But the word on the timetable is far older than the class. It comes from a single sutra, 2.29, a list of eight words. And if you read the list, you'll notice something that might surprise the six p.m. crowd. Of the eight, exactly one is a posture.
screen: `ASHTANGA, SIX P.M.` → `BRING WATER.` → `A LIST OF EIGHT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Ashta means eight. Anga means limb, a part of a body. Yesterday Patanjali said that by practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity dwindles and discernment shines. Today he lists them. Yama, the restraints: how you treat others. Niyama, the observances: how you treat yourself. Asana, the seat. Pranayama, working with the breath. Pratyahara, the senses drawing back. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation. And samadhi, absorption. Listen to the direction of that list. It starts outside, with other people, and moves steadily inward: your habits, your body, your breath, your senses, your attention, until there's only the object shining. Later, in book three, Patanjali calls the last three inner limbs, more internal than the first five. Teachers read the shape in different ways. Some hear a ladder: get the ethics right, then the body, then the mind. Others lean on the word itself. Limbs, not rungs. A child's arms and legs don't grow one after another. They grow together. The sutra doesn't settle it. What the sutra does settle is the proportion. Ethics first, twice. Posture, one word out of eight. Meditation and absorption at the end, where the whole thing is heading. Over the next days we'll take the limbs one by one. Today, just hold the whole body of it.
screen: `ASHTA: EIGHT. ANGA: LIMB.` · `FROM OTHERS, INWARD TO ABSORPTION.` · `A LADDER, OR LIMBS GROWING TOGETHER?` · `ONE POSTURE OUT OF EIGHT.` · then, large: `ASHTANGA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice walks all eight limbs in miniature. Hold a moment of goodwill toward someone, that's the first limb. Settle into feeling content with this exact moment, the second. Let your seat be steady and easy, the third. Let the breath lengthen a little, the fourth. Let sounds and sights stay in the background, the fifth. Rest your attention on one point, maybe the breath at the nostrils, the sixth. Let that attention flow without breaks, the seventh. And if it happens, let the point fill everything, the eighth. If it doesn't, that's normal. The bell holds the time.
Ashtanga. The eight parts of yoga in sutra 2.29, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption.
Your line: ethics first, twice. Today, count the eight on your fingers once, yama to samadhi, and notice which limb you've practiced least this week. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Classical yoga teaching presents the eight limbs of 2.29 as the framework of the whole practice, starting with the ethical restraints and observances, with posture and breath as preparation for meditation.

match.prompt: the eight limbs — tap the pairs.

myth: ashtanga in the sutras means a vigorous posture class
the class is a modern tradition. in 2.29, ashtanga is eight limbs, and only one is a posture.
the list moves from other people inward to absorption
yama and niyama come first; dharana, dhyana and samadhi last.
Patanjali calls the last three limbs the inner limbs
3.7: they are more internal than the first five.

fork.setup: a friend says, I want to start yoga. which limb does Patanjali's list begin with?
fork.reveal: 2.29 begins with yama, the restraints, starting with non-harm. posture is third.

original.note: Sanskrit aṣṭāṅga: aṣṭa (eight) plus aṅga (limb, part); the eight limbs of yoga in 2.29.

trapdoor: what you thought: ashtanga is a sweaty yoga class.
what it means: eight limbs of one practice, moving from ethics to absorption, with posture one part of eight.
what a scholar hears: asta plus anga; 2.29 lists them, and 3.7 sets dharana, dhyana and samadhi apart as antar-anga, the inner limbs.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 3.7 (the three are inner compared with the five before)

notes: Ashtanga Vinyasa as a modern style 'built in the twentieth century in Mysore' (Krishnamacharya, K. Pattabhi Jois): kept unnamed and general; confirm the framing is fair.
Sequential versus simultaneous readings of the limbs: presented as two long-standing readings without attribution; a Keeper may wish to name commentators.
Pranayama is described as 'working with the breath'; some will argue two limbs (asana, pranayama) involve the body. The 'one posture' claim is literal.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'almost any yoga studio' and drops the uncited 'twentieth century in Mysore' date; 3.7 is in book three but not at its start (fixed in teach and myth); cut 'both readings have long histories' and 'many teachers'.
